problem:
The entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & k & -2\end{aligned}]$
equals $-1.$ Find the value of $k.$

$k=${{field-1}}
worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & k & -2\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ k & -2\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =(2+k)-(-4+2)-(2k+2) \\  & =2+k+2-2k-2 \\  & =2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{13}^{t}={c}_{31}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{31} & =(-1)^{3+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{13}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31} \\  & =\frac{1}{2-k}\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{k-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{13}^{′}=-1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{k-2} & =-1 \\ -1\cdot (k-2) & =2 \\ k-2 & =-2 \\ k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
